title: Keeping clean: washing hands, bathing and brushing teeth
playtest: Walked through every card, game, activity and experiment as a parent reading aloud in a flat. Fixed: the three videos had no checked address, so they are left out. The hand wash now has the same six parts everywhere. Wash Time now says who keeps a tied card and what happens with no cards. The Back Teeth Race has a paper substitute for a dice and plain wording. The tongue test schedule matches its steps and its check. The cloth test uses a new square for each place. A repeated 20-second check, a second biscuit question, a plaque fill-in and a doubled crow joke were replaced. Nothing needs to be bought.

summary.text: Eat a biscuit, swish some water round your mouth, and look in a mirror. The front teeth look clean, but crumbs still sit in the grooves of the back teeth. Tiny living beings in your mouth eat those crumbs. Your child finds out what water, soap, a bath and a toothbrush each take away, and why. They learn when to wash their hands, how to brush the back teeth, and why we do it every day.
summary.art: A child holding a small mirror and a torch, looking at their own back teeth, with a half-eaten biscuit and a toothbrush on the table.

intro.hook: Open your mouth wide in front of a mirror, and shine a torch inside. Look at the tops of your back teeth. Are they flat and smooth, or do they have little hills and grooves?
intro.text: Your front teeth are thin and smooth. Your back teeth are wide, with bumps and grooves on top. The grooves help you grind food. They are also where food likes to hide. In this unit we find out where food and dirt stay on our bodies, and what takes them away. We test water, soap, a bath and a toothbrush.
intro.art: A child with a wide-open mouth in front of a bathroom mirror, a torch lighting up their bumpy back teeth.

outcomes: By the end I can say when to wash my hands: before I eat, after the toilet, after playing and after blowing my nose.
By the end I can wash my hands with soap, rubbing every part, for as long as it takes to sing Happy Birthday twice.
By the end I can say why I brush my teeth twice a day, and brush my back teeth as well as my front teeth.
By the end I can say that tiny living beings live in my mouth and on my skin, and that most of them do no harm.
By the end I can say why I take a bath: to wash off sweat, dust and old skin.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Hygiene means the things we do to keep our bodies and homes clean, so we stay well.
terms.example: Washing your hands before you eat idli is hygiene.
terms.art: A child washing their hands at a sink before a plate of idli, with soap foam on their fingers.

terms.meaning: Germs are tiny beings, too small to see. Some kinds can make us ill if they get inside us.
terms.example: Germs on your hands can get into your mouth when you eat with your fingers.
terms.art: A child's hand, with a magnifying circle showing a few tiny round and rod-shaped beings on the skin.

terms.meaning: Soap is something we rub on our skin with water. It lifts oil, dirt and germs off, so the water can carry them away.
terms.example: A bar of soap makes white foam when you rub it on wet hands.
terms.art: A bar of soap on a steel dish, with two wet hands covered in white foam above it.

terms.meaning: Plaque is a soft, sticky layer on your teeth. The tiny living beings in your mouth make it.
terms.example: In the morning, before you brush, your teeth feel fuzzy to your tongue. That fuzz is plaque.
terms.art: A big drawing of one tooth with a thin, pale yellow, fuzzy layer near the gum.

terms.meaning: Bristles are the thin, bendy hairs on a toothbrush. They reach into grooves and gaps.
terms.example: The bristles bend into the grooves on top of your back teeth.
terms.art: A close-up of a toothbrush with soft bristles bending into the grooves on top of a back tooth.

explanations.definition: Washing hands with soap and water takes away dirt and germs, so they cannot get from our hands into our mouths.
explanations.description: Your hands touch door handles, toys, the floor and your nose. Germs from those things stay on your hands. If you eat with your fingers, the germs go into your mouth. Some can give you a tummy upset or a cold. Water alone washes off loose dirt. But skin is a little oily, and oil holds on to germs. Soap lifts the oil, and the water carries it away. Rub all six parts: palms, backs of the hands, between the fingers, backs of the fingers, thumbs, and fingertips (scratch them in your palm). Rub for 20 seconds. That is Happy Birthday sung twice.
examples: Before you eat, and after you use the toilet, wash with soap.
After playing outside, or touching a pet, wash with soap.
After you blow your nose or sneeze into your hands, wash with soap.
Florence Nightingale, a nurse in England, wrote in 1859 that every nurse should wash her hands very often during the day.
explanations.context: This card says why we wash our hands, and when.
explanations.art: Six small pictures of hands being washed: palms together, backs of the hands, between the fingers, backs of the fingers, thumbs, and fingertips rubbing in a palm.

explanations.concept: What lives in your mouth, and why we brush
explanations.definition: Many kinds of tiny living beings live in every mouth. They eat leftover food on our teeth and make an acid. Brushing takes away the leftovers and the sticky plaque.
explanations.description: Your mouth is a home for tiny living beings called bacteria. They are too small to see. Most of them do you no harm. They eat what you eat, especially sugar. As they eat, they make an acid. An acid is something sour, like lemon juice. Over many days, acid can wear a hole in a tooth. The bacteria also make a sticky layer called plaque. Brushing takes off the food and the plaque. Food hides most in the grooves of the back teeth. So we brush every tooth, twice a day, for about two minutes.
examples: In the biscuit test, a swish of water cleaned the front teeth, but crumbs stayed in the grooves of the back teeth.
Holes in children's teeth are found most often on the tops of the back teeth, where the grooves are.
Around the age of six, new big back teeth come in behind the milk teeth. They are grown-up teeth, and they must last a whole life.
explanations.context: This card is about the tiny living beings in our mouths, and why we brush our teeth. It goes with the biscuit test.
explanations.art: A big friendly drawing of a back tooth with grooves, a few crumbs in the grooves, tiny round bacteria beside them, and a toothbrush coming in.

explanations.definition: A bath washes sweat, dust, oil and old skin off the whole body.
explanations.description: All day, your skin makes sweat and a little oil. Dust from the air and the floor sticks to them. Your skin also loses old skin in tiny flakes, while new skin grows underneath. A bath with water and a little soap washes all of this away. Fresh sweat has almost no smell. The smell comes from tiny living beings on your skin, who eat the sweat. A bath washes most of the sweat away, so the smell goes too.
examples: In the white cloth test, the sole of a foot often left a grey mark before the bath, and almost none after it.
After playing in the sun, you may feel sticky and want a second bath.
Your skin feels sticky and salty after a hot game. That is dried sweat.
explanations.context: This card says why we take a bath. It goes with the white cloth test.
explanations.art: A child pouring a mug of water from a bucket over their shoulders in a bathroom, with soap on a dish nearby.

explanations.concept: Are the tiny beings on us friends or enemies?
explanations.description: We often call all tiny living beings germs, as if they were all enemies. But most bacteria on your skin and in your mouth do you no harm. Many of them help you. Some keep harmful kinds away just by living in their place. Only a few kinds make us ill. So washing and brushing do not try to remove every tiny being. They keep the numbers small, and keep harmful kinds out of our mouths. Bacteria also send each other chemical signals. Scientists think these signals help them build a sticky layer like plaque.
examples: Plaque grows back on your teeth every night. Brushing keeps it thin.
Bacteria on healthy skin help keep harmful bacteria from settling there.
Curd is made by helpful bacteria.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the bacteria living on and in us
perspectives.explanation: Most of these bacteria are our neighbours, not our enemies. A body is a home for many beings, and good hygiene keeps that home in balance.
Some of these bacteria do cause holes in teeth and illness. So we should think of them as germs to keep off, and wash and brush well every day.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how bacteria behave
perspectives.explanation: Bacteria sense each other and act together, which is why they build plaque only when there are many of them. Some scientists call this decision-making. Others call it automatic chemistry.

explanations.context: This card asks whether the tiny living beings on our bodies are friends or enemies. Scientists see it in different ways.
explanations.art: A child's smiling face with a magnifying circle on the cheek and one on a tooth, each showing many small, friendly round beings and one or two spiky ones.

explanations.concept: Humans and other animals keep clean
explanations.definition: Many animals, including humans, spend time every day cleaning their bodies.
explanations.description: Humans are not the only animals who keep clean. A cat licks her fur with a rough tongue. A crow dips into water and shakes her feathers. A sparrow rolls in dry dust, and the dust takes extra oil off her feathers. An elephant sprays water and mud over her back. An ant has a tiny comb on each front leg, and she pulls her feelers through it to clean them. Monkeys pick through each other's fur. Humans use water, soap and toothbrushes. Each animal cleans in the way that suits their body.
examples: A crow or pigeon may bathe in a dish of water left on a balcony.
A cat licks her paws, then wipes her face with them.
Elephants at temple and forest camps in Kerala and Karnataka are given baths in rivers.
explanations.context: This card says that many animals, humans among them, keep their bodies clean.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a row: a cat licking her paw, a crow splashing in a dish of water, a sparrow in a dust bath, an elephant spraying water, and a child brushing their teeth.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap and water stops many illnesses from spreading.
agreed.evidence: In a study in Karachi, in Pakistan, families were given soap and shown how to wash their hands. Their children had about half as many tummy upsets with diarrhoea, and about half as many chest infections, as children in other families.

agreed.text: Brushing twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste helps stop holes in teeth.
agreed.evidence: Dentists have compared large groups of children for many years. Children who brushed twice a day with fluoride toothpaste got fewer holes in their teeth.

agreed.text: Bacteria in the mouth make acid from sugar, and the acid wears away teeth.
agreed.evidence: In 1890, Willoughby Miller showed in a laboratory that mouth bacteria given sugar make acid, and that the acid softens teeth.

challenging.for: Scrubbing hard cleans a dirty floor or a pot faster.
challenging.against: Teeth and gums are not a floor. Plaque is soft and comes off with gentle brushing. Brushing very hard can hurt the gums and wear the teeth. Dentists say: a soft brush, small gentle circles, and every part of every tooth.
challenging.context: This card is about how hard to brush your teeth.

challenging.claim: Children are healthier if they play in some dirt, so too much cleaning is bad.
challenging.for: Children who grow up on farms, with animals and soil, get some allergies less often. Our bodies may need to meet many harmless microbes when we are young.
challenging.against: This does not mean dirty hands are good. Washing hands before eating and after the toilet still stops many illnesses. Scientists are still working out which kinds of contact with nature help, and how.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a little dirt can be good for children.

challenging.claim: Milk teeth fall out anyway, so they do not need brushing.
challenging.for: Milk teeth do fall out, between about age 6 and age 12.
challenging.against: A hole in a milk tooth can hurt and make eating hard. Milk teeth hold the space for the grown-up teeth growing underneath. And the big back teeth that come in at about age six are grown-up teeth already.
challenging.context: This card is about whether milk teeth need care.

big_questions.q: Every time you eat, the tiny beings in your mouth eat too. Is your mouth only yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about who lives there, and what they eat.

big_questions.q: Your old skin comes off in tiny flakes, and new skin grows underneath. Is your skin today the same skin you had last year?
big_questions.hint: Think about the flakes in the bath water.

big_questions.q: A cat licks, a sparrow rolls in dust, and you use soap. Why do so many animals spend time keeping clean?
big_questions.hint: Think about what dirt, oil and tiny beings do to fur, feathers and skin.

big_questions.q: The water that washes your hands goes down the drain. Where does it go next, and who meets it there?
big_questions.hint: Think about pipes, rivers, the sea, and the living beings in them.

story.title: The Tooth at the Back
story.note: Revathi, her mother and her grandfather are made up. It is true that the first big grown-up back teeth usually come in at about age six, behind the milk teeth, and that their grooves are where food stays most.
text: Revathi was six. She lived in Thrissur, in Kerala, with her mother and her grandfather. She called her grandfather Appooppan. Every morning, the three of them ate breakfast together on the floor of the kitchen.
One morning there was puttu, soft and white and steaming, with black kadala curry. Revathi loved puttu. She pressed it into the curry with her fingers and ate a big mouthful.
Then she stopped chewing. Her tongue had found something new. Right at the back of her mouth, behind all her small teeth, there was something hard and wide.
'Amma,' she said. 'There is a stone in my mouth.'
Amma laughed. She fetched the torch from the shelf. 'Open wide,' she said, and she shone the light inside.
'That is not a stone,' said Amma. 'That is a new tooth. It is a big grown-up tooth, coming in behind your milk teeth. Most children get one at about your age, on each side, top and bottom.'

Revathi went to the mirror by the door. Amma held the torch. Revathi pulled her cheek back with one finger. There it was: a wide white tooth, bigger than all the others. On top, it had little hills and valleys, like a tiny mountain range.
And in the valleys, there was puttu.
'There is breakfast in my tooth,' said Revathi.
'Swish some water and look again,' said Amma.

Revathi took a big sip from the steel tumbler. She swished it round her mouth, puffing out her cheeks, and spat into the sink. She looked again. Her front teeth were clean. But in the valleys of the new tooth, little white crumbs of puttu were still sitting there.
'The water went over the top,' said Revathi. 'It didn't go into the valleys.'

'Those valleys are called grooves,' said Amma. 'They help you grind food. But food hides in them. Tiny living beings in your mouth find it there and eat it. They make an acid as they eat, and the acid can make a hole in the tooth. So we have to clean the grooves.'
'How?' said Revathi.
Amma gave her the toothbrush. 'Put the bristles right on top of the back tooth,' she said. 'Brush gently, back and forth, in short little strokes. Let the bristles go down into the grooves.'
Revathi brushed. Then she looked in the mirror again, with the torch. The grooves were clean. She ran her tongue over the new tooth. It felt smooth and squeaky.
'This tooth has to last you your whole life,' said Amma. 'It will never be swapped for a new one.'
Revathi thought about that all day.
That evening, after dinner, Appooppan drank a glass of water, swished it round his mouth, and went to sit on the verandah. Revathi followed him with the torch.
'Appooppan,' she said. 'Open wide, please.'
Appooppan smiled and opened his mouth. Revathi shone the torch on his back teeth. They had grooves too, big ones. And in the grooves there was rice from dinner.
'Appooppan, the water went over the top,' said Revathi. 'The rice is still in the grooves.'
Appooppan looked surprised. 'I have rinsed with water after every meal for seventy years,' he said.
'Water is good,' said Revathi, the way Amma said it. 'But it doesn't reach the grooves. You need bristles.'
Appooppan cleaned his teeth every morning with a neem twig. He chewed one end until it was soft and spread out, like a little brush. Revathi watched him do it the next morning.
'You only do the front,' she said. 'Do the back teeth too. On the top. That is where the food hides.'

So Appooppan reached the soft end of the twig right to the back of his mouth. He rubbed the tops of his back teeth slowly. Revathi held the torch, and he looked in the mirror. 'Well,' he said. 'You are right. The back was hiding things from me.'

From then on, every night, Revathi and Appooppan stood at the sink together. Revathi had her toothbrush. Appooppan had his own brush now, a soft one that Amma bought him from the shop. Revathi counted while they brushed: the top left, the top right, the bottom left, the bottom right. The front teeth, and the back teeth, and the grooves.
And every morning, before they brushed, they both ran their tongues over their teeth, and made a face. 'Fuzzy,' said Revathi. 'Fuzzy,' said Appooppan. The tiny beings had been busy all night.
'Again,' said Revathi, and handed him his brush.
story.epiphany: Revathi sees that water runs over the top of a tooth, but bristles reach into the grooves where food hides. The part of the mouth we cannot see easily is the part that needs the most care.
ask: Why did the water clean Revathi's front teeth but not the grooves of her new tooth?
Why did Amma say the new back tooth has to last a whole life?
Why do you think the teeth felt fuzzy again every morning?
Have you found any big new back teeth in your mouth yet?

games.title: Wash Time! A card game about when to wash
games.context: This is a card game about when to wash our hands with soap. Each card shows a moment in the day. If it is a time to wash, everyone pretends to wash their hands, as fast as they can.

items.b: Wash! Your fingers will carry food to your mouth.
Wash! Germs from the toilet can get on your hands.

items.f: After playing in the park or on the balcony
items.b: Wash! Hands pick up dust and germs while you play.
Wash! Germs from your nose are now on your hands.
Wash! A sneeze sprays germs onto your hands.

items.f: After stroking a dog or a cat
items.b: Wash! Fur carries dirt and tiny beings.

items.f: Before helping to make chapatis or dosa batter
items.b: Wash! Your hands will touch food that others eat.
Wash! Rubbish is full of germs.

items.f: After coming home from the market
items.b: Wash! You touched many things that many people touched.
Wash! Even if you peel it, your fingers touch the fruit you eat.

items.f: Reading a book on the sofa
items.b: No wash needed now. Wash before you eat later.
No wash needed. Singing does not make hands dirty.
No wash needed. They are already clean!
No wash needed yet. Brush your teeth soon!

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Mix them and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. A grown-up reads it for a child who cannot read yet.
If it is a time to wash, everyone rubs their hands as if washing. The first to start keeps the card. If you start together, the child keeps it.
If it is not a time to wash, everyone keeps still. Anyone who moves their hands puts one of their cards back at the bottom of the pile. If you have no cards yet, nothing happens.
Read the back of the card aloud to check.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most cards wins. Then everyone does one real hand wash together.

setup.art: A pile of small paper cards face down on a mat, with three players sitting round it.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while a child rubs their hands together fast and another player sits still.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card. Wash time? Rub your hands fast!

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Mix them and stack them face down. 3. Explain the rules.
flow.say: Each card shows a moment in the day. If it is a time to wash your hands, rub your hands as fast as you can. If not, keep very still.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Is it a time to wash? Rub your hands fast! If not, keep still.

flow.do: Take turns to turn a card and read it. Everyone washes or keeps still. Read the back to check.
flow.say: Is this a time to wash? Why? Let's read the back.
flow.kid: Wash or keep still? Say why. Read the back.

check.q: The card says 'After stroking a dog or a cat'. Wash or keep still?
check.why: Fur carries dirt and tiny beings onto your hands, so it is a time to wash.

flow.do: Count the cards. Then everyone does one real six-part hand wash.
flow.say: Who has the most cards? Now let's all do a real wash, with soap, and sing Happy Birthday twice.
flow.kid: Count your cards. Now do a real wash, with soap!

games.title: Back Teeth Race: a board game
games.context: This is a race along a path of 20 teeth. Some squares help you, because you cleaned well. Some send you back, because food was left behind. The first to reach the last tooth wins.

printables.title: 20 tooth squares to draw in a winding path
items: 1. Start: you woke up. Your teeth feel fuzzy.
3. You brushed your back teeth. Jump forward 2.
5. You forgot to brush at night. Go back 2.
7. You swished water after a sweet. Forward 1.
9. Crumbs stuck in a groove. Miss a turn.
11. You brushed for two whole minutes. Forward 3.
13. You ate sweets all afternoon. Go back 3.
15. You used a soft brush and small gentle strokes. Forward 2.
17. You only brushed the front teeth. Go back 2.
19. You used a pea-sized bit of toothpaste. Forward 1.
20. Finish: a clean, smooth back tooth!

rules: Draw the 20 squares as a winding path of teeth on a big sheet. Write or draw what each square says.
Each player puts their token on square 1.
Take turns to throw a dice (from a ludo set). No dice? Write 1, 2 and 3 on three bits of paper, fold them, and pick one each turn. Move that many squares.
If you land on a square with a message, a grown-up reads it, and you do what it says.
If a square sends you back past square 1, stay on square 1.
The first player to reach square 20 wins. You do not need the exact number to finish.
Playing alone? Race against your own best: count how many throws you need, and try to beat it next time.

setup.caption: 2. Throw the dice, move, and do what the square says.

flow.do: 1. Draw the path and write the squares. 2. Cut out the tokens. 3. Find a dice.
flow.say: This is a race along 20 teeth. Good cleaning helps you forward. Food left behind sends you back.
flow.kid: Draw the path of teeth. Pick a token. Find a dice.

flow.do: Play, taking turns. When someone lands on a message, ask why it helps or why it sends them back.
flow.say: You landed on 'You only brushed the front teeth'. Why does that send you back?
flow.kid: Throw the dice. Move. Do what the square says. Say why.

check.q: Why does 'Crumbs stuck in a groove' make you miss a turn?
options: The tiny beings in your mouth eat the crumbs and make acid
Crumbs make your tooth fall out at once
check.why: Crumbs left in a groove feed the tiny beings in your mouth. They make an acid, which can wear a hole in the tooth over many days.

flow.do: The first to reach square 20 wins.
flow.say: You reached the clean back tooth! What helped you most on the way?
flow.kid: Who reached the clean tooth first? What helped most?

items.p: In the Biscuit Test, you ate a biscuit and swished water round your mouth. Draw a back tooth. Draw where the crumbs stayed after the swish.
items.a: A wide tooth with grooves on top, and crumbs drawn inside the grooves.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the grooves on top of the back tooth and puts the crumbs inside them, because that is where water did not reach.
items.art: An empty box with the outline of a wide back tooth.

items.p: Colour the times to wash your hands green. Colour the other times yellow.
items.why: We wash before eating, after the toilet, after blowing our nose and after playing, because those are the times germs get on our hands or into our mouths. Listening and looking do not make hands dirty.
items.art: Six small pictures: a plate of food, a toilet, a child blowing their nose, a radio, a child on a slide, a child looking at the sky.

items.p: You have a new big tooth at the back, with little hills and valleys on top. After you eat puttu, where is the food most likely to hide?
opts: In the grooves on top of the tooth
On the tip of your tongue
items.why: A back tooth has little hills and valleys on top. Food hides in those valleys, which are called grooves.

items.p: Put the hand wash in order.
items.why: First wet the hands so the soap can foam. Then rub every part. Then rinse the soap away with the dirt in it. Last, dry.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to what it cleans.
items.why: A toothbrush reaches the grooves of the teeth. Soap lifts dirt off hands. A nail cutter makes short nails, which leave less space for dirt. A bath washes sweat and dust off the whole body.
items.art: Four pictures on the left: a toothbrush, soap, a nail cutter, a bucket and mug. Four labels on the right.

items.p: Skin that looks clean has no dirt on it at all.
items.why: False. In the white cloth test, skin that looked clean still made the cloth grey before a bath. Dust and sweat can be too thin to see.

items.p: Here are two hands. Put a tick on the parts people often forget to wash: the thumbs, the fingertips and the backs of the hands.
items.a: Ticks on both thumbs, the fingertips and the backs of both hands.
items.why: Most people rub their palms well, but miss the thumbs, the fingertips and the backs. A strong answer ticks all three.
items.art: An outline of two hands, palms down, with the thumbs and fingertips clearly drawn.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: why do we wash our hands before we eat?
items.a: Because germs on our hands can go into our mouth with the food.
items.why: A strong answer says that our hands carry germs, and that eating with our hands takes them to our mouth.

items.p: If you only brush your front teeth, what are you missing?
opts: The back teeth, where food hides
items.why: Food hides most in the grooves of the back teeth. Holes in children's teeth are found most often there. If you picked 'the front is enough', remember the Biscuit Test: after a swish of water, crumbs stayed in the grooves of the back teeth.

items.p: Draw yourself having a bath. Draw what the water is washing off you.
items.a: A child pouring water or under a shower, with dust, sweat drops or tiny flakes washing off.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water carrying something away: sweat, dust, or tiny flakes of old skin.

items.p: Farida, a girl of 7 in Hyderabad, and her uncle Imran are talking about brushing.

views.says: I brush my back teeth every night, because the tiny beings in my mouth eat the leftover food.
I rinse my mouth with water after every meal. That is enough to keep teeth clean.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the biscuit test. For example: 'Farida, because water left crumbs in my back teeth, and the brush took them out.' Then it is fair to Uncle Imran: rinsing does wash the front teeth and helps a little.
items.why: Both are partly right. Rinsing helps, especially after sweets. But in the biscuit test, only the brush cleaned the grooves of the back teeth.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: in the morning your teeth feel fuzzy. What is the fuzz, and why does it come back every night?
items.a: The fuzz is plaque. Tiny living beings in my mouth build it while I sleep, so it grows back every night.
items.why: A strong answer names plaque, says it is made by the tiny beings who live in the mouth, and says they build it again each night, so we brush every day.

items.p: Why do we use soap, and not only water, to wash our hands?
opts: Soap lifts the oily layer that holds dirt and germs
Soap makes hands smell nice, and that is all
items.why: Skin is a little oily, and the oil holds dirt and germs. Water slides over the oil. Soap lifts the oil off so the water can carry it away. A nice smell is not what cleans.

items.p: Three of these keep clean by washing or licking. Which one keeps clean by rolling in dry dust?
items.why: A sparrow takes a dust bath. A cat licks her fur, an elephant sprays water, and a child uses soap and water.

items.p: Brushing very hard is the best way to clean your teeth.
items.why: False. Plaque is soft, so gentle brushing takes it off. Hard brushing can hurt the gums and wear the teeth.

items.p: Only humans keep their bodies clean.
items.why: False. A cat licks her fur, a crow splashes in water, a sparrow rolls in dust, and an elephant sprays water over her back.

items.p: Draw your mouth as a home. Who lives there? What do they eat?
items.a: A mouth with teeth, and tiny beings drawn on and between the teeth, with crumbs of food near them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that tiny living beings live in the mouth and feed on leftover food. Extra marks for drawing food in the grooves of the back teeth.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: milk teeth fall out. Why should we still brush them?
items.a: A hole in a milk tooth can hurt. Milk teeth keep space for the grown-up teeth. And the big back teeth that come at about age six are grown-up teeth already.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least one real reason: holes hurt, milk teeth hold the space, or the six-year back teeth are grown-up teeth that stay for life.

items.p: Socks can smell after a hot day. Where does the smell come from?
opts: Tiny beings on the skin, who feed on sweat
The sweat itself, which always smells strong
items.why: Fresh sweat has almost no smell. The smell is made by tiny living beings on the skin who feed on the sweat. A bath and clean socks wash most of them and the sweat away.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a mouth, seen from above. Write F on the front teeth and B on the back teeth. Put a star where food hides most.
items.a: F on the front teeth, B on the wide back teeth, and a star on the tops of the back teeth.
items.why: The grooves on top of the back teeth are where food stays most, as the biscuit test showed.
items.art: A U-shaped row of teeth seen from above, with thin teeth at the front and wide teeth at the back.

experiments.title: The Biscuit Test: what does a rinse clean, and what does a brush clean?
experiments.context: In this experiment you eat a biscuit, then look at your teeth with a mirror and a torch. You rinse with water and look again. Then you brush and look again. You find out where food stays, and what takes it away.
experiments.question: After we eat, does a swish of water clean all our teeth? Or does some food stay behind, and where?
experiments.predict: After you eat a biscuit, will a swish of water wash all the crumbs away? Where do you think crumbs might stay? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We look at the same teeth each time, with the same torch and mirror. We look three times: after eating, after rinsing, and after brushing. Only one thing changes each time: what we clean with.

materials.item: a biscuit (a dark one, like a ragi or chocolate biscuit, shows best)
a mirror (a hand mirror, or the bathroom mirror)
a torch, or the torch on a phone
a steel tumbler of drinking water
your child's own toothbrush
a sheet of paper and two crayons of different colours

schedule.what: Look at the teeth. Eat a biscuit, rinse with water, then brush. Look at the teeth again after each step.

experiments.record: A tooth map: draw a big U shape for the teeth. Use one colour to mark where crumbs were after rinsing. Use a second colour to mark where crumbs were after brushing.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Lots of brown paste in the grooves

setup.art: A child holding a mirror while a grown-up shines a torch into the child's open mouth, showing the bumpy tops of the back teeth.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the front teeth and the back teeth with a torch.

setup.art: A child chewing a dark biscuit, then looking in the mirror at brown crumbs in the grooves of the back teeth.
setup.caption: 2. Eat the biscuit. Look again.

setup.art: A child puffing out their cheeks to swish water, beside a steel tumbler and a sink.
setup.caption: 3. Swish water and spit. Look again.

setup.art: A child brushing the top of a back tooth with a small toothbrush, the bristles bending into the grooves.
setup.caption: 4. Brush gently. Look one last time.

flow.do: 1. Shine the torch into your child's mouth while they hold the mirror. 2. Find the front teeth and the back teeth together. 3. Draw a big U on the paper. Mark F at the front and B at each back end.
flow.say: Let's look inside your mouth. These are your front teeth. They are thin and smooth. These are your back teeth. Look at the tops. What do you see?
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Find your front teeth. Now find your back teeth. Look at their tops.

ask.q: What are the tops of the back teeth like?
good: They have little hills and lines.

flow.parent: The tops of the back teeth have grooves. Children often have never looked at them. Let your child take their time.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before they eat. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Soon you will eat a biscuit. Then you will swish water round your mouth. Will the water wash all the crumbs away? Where might crumbs stay? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will eat a biscuit, then swish water. Will the water clean every tooth? Guess. Say why.

good: Water washes things, so it will all go.
The crumbs might stick in the bumpy bits.
The back is hard to reach.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not give the answer. Many children guess that water will wash everything away.

flow.do: 1. Your child eats the biscuit and chews it well. 2. No drinking yet. 3. Shine the torch and look at the front teeth, the tops of the back teeth, and between the teeth.
flow.say: Eat the biscuit and chew it well. Don't drink anything yet. Now open wide. Where can you see crumbs?
flow.kid: Eat the biscuit. Chew it well. Don't drink yet. Open wide. Where are the crumbs?
flow.parent: You will usually see brown paste on the tops of the back teeth, and a little on the front teeth and between them.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a big sip of water. 2. They swish it hard round the mouth while you count to ten. 3. They spit it into the sink. 4. Do it once more. 5. Look again with the torch. 6. Colour any crumbs on the tooth map in the first colour.
flow.say: Take a big sip. Swish it all round while I count to ten. Spit. Once more. Now open wide. What has gone, and what is still there?
flow.kid: Take a big sip. Swish it round. Count to ten. Spit. Do it again. Look. What is still there?

ask.q: What did the water clean? What did it leave?
good: There are still crumbs in the grooves of the back teeth.
Some crumbs are still between my teeth.

flow.parent: Crumbs usually stay in the grooves of the back teeth and between the teeth. If the water cleaned everything, try again another day with a stickier food, such as a piece of chikki or a date.

flow.do: 1. Your child brushes with their toothbrush and a little water, or a smear of toothpaste. 2. Remind them to put the bristles on top of the back teeth. 3. Brush gently for about one minute. 4. Look again. 5. Colour anything left in the second colour.
flow.say: Now brush. Put the bristles right on top of the back teeth. Brush gently, back and forth. Now let's look. What is left?
flow.kid: Brush your teeth. Put the bristles on top of the back teeth. Brush gently. Now look. What is left?

ask.q: What did the brush clean that the water did not?
good: The grooves on the back teeth.

flow.parent: The grooves are usually clean now. A tiny bit may stay between two teeth. A grown-up can clean between teeth with dental floss, if you have some.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. Then read the tooth map together.
flow.say: So what do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think the water left crumbs in the grooves, and the brush took them out?
flow.kid: What did you find out? What did you see? Why did the brush work better at the back?

ask.q: Why did the brush clean the grooves?
good: The bristles go down into the grooves.
Water just goes over the top.
The brush rubs, and water only washes.

check.q: After the water rinse, where were crumbs most likely to stay?
options: In the grooves of the back teeth
check.why: Water runs over the smooth front teeth and washes them. It flows over the grooves of the back teeth without reaching inside, so crumbs stay there. If you picked the front teeth, look again at the tooth map: the front teeth were clean after the rinse.

flow.think: Tiny living beings in your mouth eat leftover crumbs. Where in your mouth would they find the most food?

experiments.title: The White Cloth Test: what does a bath wash off?
experiments.context: In this experiment you wipe a damp white cloth on your skin before a bath, and again after it. You look at the cloth to see what the bath took away.
experiments.question: Does our skin carry dirt we cannot see? Does a bath take it away?
experiments.predict: Your skin looks clean. If we wipe it with a white cloth before your bath, will the cloth get dirty? What about after the bath? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We wipe the same three places each time: the back of the neck, the inside of the elbow and the sole of one foot. We use the same kind of cloth, made just damp, and wipe each place three times. Each place gets a new square of cloth.
results_table: Before the bath: mark on the cloth?
After the bath: mark on the cloth?

materials.item: an old white cotton cloth, hanky or vest, cut into 6 small squares (or 6 balls of cotton wool)
a small katori of clean water
a sheet of paper to lay the cloth squares on

schedule.what: Wipe three places before the bath and three after. Compare the cloths.

experiments.record: Lay the six cloth squares on paper in two rows: before the bath and after the bath. Draw them, or keep them dry in an envelope.

setup.art: A grown-up wiping the back of a child's neck with a small damp white cloth square, with two more squares on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Before the bath, wipe the neck, the elbow and the sole of a foot.

setup.art: Two rows of white cloth squares on paper: the top row grey and brown in places, the bottom row almost white.
setup.caption: 2. After the bath, wipe the same places. Compare the rows.

flow.do: Before the bath, ask your child to guess. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Your skin looks clean. If I wipe it with a white cloth, will the cloth get dirty? Where might it get most dirty? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Your skin looks clean. Will a white cloth get dirty on it? Guess. Say why.

good: I played outside, so I might be dusty.
My feet walk on the floor.
My skin looks clean, so the cloth will stay white.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not tell your child the answer.

flow.do: 1. Dip a cloth square in the water and squeeze it until just damp. 2. Wipe the back of the neck three times. 3. Put the square on the paper. 4. Do the same with a new square on the inside of the elbow, and on the sole of one foot.
flow.say: I am wiping the back of your neck. One, two, three. Now your elbow. Now the bottom of your foot. Let's put the cloths in a row.
flow.kid: Wipe the back of your neck three times. Then your elbow. Then the bottom of your foot. Put the cloths in a row.
flow.parent: The sole of a foot that has walked barefoot at home almost always leaves a grey mark. The neck often leaves a faint brown or grey mark, especially after playing outside or a sweaty day.

flow.do: 1. Your child has their bath as usual, with soap. 2. After drying, wipe the same three places with three new damp squares. 3. Put them in a second row under the first.
flow.say: Now you have had your bath. Let's wipe the same places again, with new cloths. Neck, elbow, foot.
flow.kid: After your bath, wipe the same three places. Use new cloths. Put them in a second row.
flow.parent: The time for the bath is not counted in the time for this experiment. Do this step right after drying, before the feet walk on the floor again.

flow.do: Look at the two rows together. Ask your child what they think, what they see, and why.
flow.say: Look at the two rows. Which cloths are dirtier? What do you think the bath took away? Why?
flow.kid: Look at both rows. Which cloths are dirty? What did the bath take away?

ask.q: What did the bath wash off?

check.q: Which row of cloths was more likely to be grey?
options: The row from before the bath
The row from after the bath
check.why: Before a bath, dust sticks to the sweat and oil on your skin. A bath with soap washes them off, so the second row is cleaner. If your rows looked the same, your skin may have been clean already. Try again after a day of playing.

experiments.title: The Morning Tongue Test: does the fuzz come back?
experiments.context: In this experiment you feel your teeth with your tongue in the morning, before and after brushing. You do it two mornings in a row. You find out if the fuzzy feeling comes back.
experiments.question: Our teeth feel fuzzy in the morning. After we brush, does the fuzz stay away, or does it come back?
experiments.predict: After you brush tonight, will your teeth feel fuzzy again tomorrow morning? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each time, we feel the same teeth, the back teeth, with the tongue. We feel them at the same two times each morning: right after waking up, and right after brushing.

materials.item: your child's own toothbrush and toothpaste
a sheet of paper with two rows of two boxes drawn on it
a crayon

schedule.what: The night before, guess. In the morning, feel the back teeth before brushing. Brush. Feel again. Colour the boxes.
Do the same again. Has the fuzz come back?

experiments.record: Two rows of two boxes. Draw a wavy line in a box for fuzzy, and a smooth line for smooth.

setup.art: A sleepy child just out of bed, running their tongue over their teeth with a puzzled face.
setup.caption: 1. When you wake up, feel your back teeth with your tongue.

setup.art: A child brushing their teeth at a sink, then smiling and touching their tongue to their teeth.
setup.caption: 2. Brush. Then feel again. Do it again the next morning.

flow.do: The night before, ask your child to guess. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Tomorrow morning, before you brush, feel your back teeth with your tongue. Will they feel smooth or fuzzy? And after you brush? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tomorrow morning, feel your teeth with your tongue. Smooth or fuzzy? Guess. Say why.

good: I brushed tonight, so they will be smooth.
They always feel funny in the morning.

flow.do: 1. On the first morning, before brushing, your child runs their tongue over the back teeth. 2. They draw a wavy or smooth line. 3. They brush. 4. They feel again and draw again.
flow.say: Before you brush, run your tongue over your back teeth. Smooth or fuzzy? Now brush. Feel again. Smooth or fuzzy?
flow.kid: Feel your back teeth with your tongue. Smooth or fuzzy? Draw it. Now brush. Feel again. Draw it.
flow.wait: Do the next step tomorrow morning, before brushing.
flow.parent: Most people feel a soft fuzz in the morning, mainly near the gums. After brushing, the teeth feel smooth and squeaky.

flow.do: 1. On the second morning, feel the back teeth again before brushing. 2. Draw it. 3. Brush and feel again. 4. Talk about what you found.
flow.say: You brushed last night. Is the fuzz back this morning? What do you think the fuzz is? Why does it come back?
flow.kid: Feel your back teeth again. Is the fuzz back? What do you think the fuzz is?

ask.q: Why did the fuzz come back?
good: Something grew on my teeth at night.
The tiny living beings in my mouth made it again.
It is plaque, and it grows back.

check.q: What is the fuzz on your teeth in the morning?
options: Plaque, a sticky layer made by tiny living beings
check.why: The fuzz is plaque. The bacteria in your mouth build this sticky layer. It grows back every night, so we brush every day. If you picked toothpaste, remember that the fuzz came back even though you brushed the night before.

activities.title: The Six-Part Hand Wash, with a song
activities.context: In this activity you learn to wash every part of your hands with soap, while you sing Happy Birthday twice.

materials.item: soap (a bar or liquid soap)
a tap, or a mug of water and a bucket
a clean towel

schedule.what: Learn the six parts of a hand wash. Wash while singing Happy Birthday twice.

activities.record: Draw your two hands. Colour the part that is easiest to forget.

setup.art: Two soapy hands rubbing palm to palm, then one palm rubbing over the back of the other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Palms together. Then the backs of the hands.

setup.art: Two soapy hands with fingers laced together, then one hand twisting round the other thumb, then fingertips rubbing in a palm.
setup.caption: 2. Between the fingers. The thumbs. The fingertips and nails.

setup.art: Hands being rinsed under a tap and dried on a towel.
setup.caption: 3. Rinse well. Dry on a clean towel.

flow.do: 1. Wet your hands and your child's hands. 2. Rub soap until it foams. 3. Show the six parts slowly: palms, backs, between the fingers, backs of the fingers, thumbs, fingertips in the palm.
flow.say: Watch my hands. Palms together. Backs of the hands. Fingers in between each other. Backs of the fingers. Each thumb. Now the fingertips, scratching in the palm.
flow.kid: Wet your hands. Rub on soap. Palms. Backs. Between the fingers. Backs of the fingers. Thumbs. Fingertips.
flow.parent: The thumbs, the fingertips and the backs of the hands are the parts most people forget.

flow.do: 1. Now your child washes alone, doing all six parts. 2. Sing Happy Birthday twice together while they rub. 3. Rinse and dry.
flow.say: Now you do it. We will sing Happy Birthday two times. Keep rubbing until the song ends. Then rinse and dry.
flow.kid: Wash all six parts. Sing Happy Birthday two times. Keep rubbing until the end. Rinse. Dry.

ask.q: Which part did you nearly forget?

flow.do: Talk about when to wash hands with soap.
flow.say: When do you think we should wash our hands with soap? Why then?
flow.kid: When should you wash your hands? Say as many times as you can.

ask.q: When do we wash our hands?

activities.title: What Hides Under Your Nails?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up gently cleans under your nails onto white paper. You see what was hiding there. Then you scrub your nails and look again.
activities.safety: A grown-up holds the toothpick and the nail cutter.

materials.item: a sheet of white paper
a toothpick
soap and an old, clean toothbrush
a nail cutter

schedule.what: Clean under the nails onto paper. Scrub. Look again. Trim the nails.

activities.record: Circle the grey bits on the paper with a crayon, and write the date.

setup.art: A grown-up gently running a toothpick under a child's fingernail, over a sheet of white paper with tiny grey bits on it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cleans under each nail onto white paper.

setup.art: A child scrubbing their fingertips with soap and an old toothbrush at a sink.
setup.caption: 2. Scrub your nails with soap and an old brush.

flow.do: 1. Do this after your child has played. 2. Hold your child's hand over the white paper. 3. Gently run the toothpick under each nail, without pushing in. 4. Look at the paper.
flow.say: Your nails look clean. What do you think is hiding under them? Let's see. Now look at the paper.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to help. Hold your hand over the paper. What falls out from under your nails?

ask.q: What can you see on the paper?

flow.parent: Work gently and only at the very edge of the nail. After play, there are almost always small grey bits of dirt.

flow.do: 1. Your child wets their hands and rubs soap on the old toothbrush. 2. They scrub the tips of their fingers and nails. 3. Rinse, dry, and check under one nail again.
flow.say: Now scrub your nails with soap and the brush. Let's look under one nail again. What do you see now?
flow.kid: Scrub your nails with soap and the old brush. Rinse. Look again. Are they clean now?

ask.q: Why do you think dirt hides under nails?
good: There is a little gap there.
We dig and touch things with our fingertips.

flow.do: A grown-up trims your child's nails short with the nail cutter.
flow.say: Short nails have less space for dirt to hide. Let's trim them.
flow.kid: A grown-up trims your nails short. Then there is less space for dirt.
flow.parent: Trim straight across, not too close to the skin.

activities.title: Who Else Keeps Clean?
activities.context: In this activity you watch for animals keeping clean, and act out how each one does it. Humans are one of many animals who keep clean.

materials.item: a window or balcony where crows, pigeons or sparrows come, if you have one
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Act out five animals keeping clean. Watch for a bird or an ant cleaning, if one is there.

activities.record: Draw one animal keeping clean, and yourself keeping clean.

setup.art: A child licking the back of their hand and wiping their face, pretending to be a cat, while a grown-up laughs.
setup.caption: 1. Act out a cat, a crow, a sparrow, an elephant and an ant.

setup.art: A crow on a balcony rail fluffing up her wet feathers next to a shallow dish of water.
setup.caption: 2. Watch at the window. Who is keeping clean?

flow.do: 1. Name each animal. 2. Ask your child to guess how that animal keeps clean. 3. Then tell them, and you both act it out.
flow.say: How do you think a cat keeps clean? She licks her fur. A sparrow rolls in dry dust. An elephant sprays water with her trunk. An ant pulls her feelers through a tiny comb on her front leg.
flow.kid: How does a cat keep clean? Act it out. Now a sparrow in the dust. Now an elephant spraying water.

ask.q: Why do you think animals keep clean?
good: So their fur and feathers work well.
To get rid of dirt and tiny bugs.

flow.parent: Other animals clean in the way that suits their bodies. Humans use water and soap, and brush with a toothbrush.

flow.do: 1. Look out of the window or at the balcony for a minute or two. 2. Look for a bird combing their feathers with their beak (this is called preening), or an ant cleaning her feelers. 3. Draw what you saw, or draw your favourite animal from the game.
flow.say: Let's watch the window for a little while. Can you see a bird combing their feathers with their beak?
flow.kid: Look out of the window. Is a bird combing their feathers with their beak? Draw what you see.
flow.parent: Crows and pigeons often preen on ledges. If no bird comes, that is fine: draw an animal from the acting game. If you leave a shallow dish of water on the balcony, a crow or pigeon may come to bathe over the next few days.

activities.title: Mine, Not Shared: my own clean-up kit
activities.context: In this activity you sort the things your family uses to keep clean. You find out which ones each person should have for themselves.

materials.item: things from the bathroom: a toothbrush, a towel, a comb, a bar of soap, a nail cutter, a bucket and mug

schedule.what: Say what each thing is for. Sort them into 'only mine' and 'we can share'.

activities.record: Draw your own toothbrush and towel, with your name on them.

setup.art: A toothbrush, a towel, a comb, a bar of soap, a nail cutter and a mug laid out on a mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the things. Say what each is for.

setup.art: Two mats: one labelled 'only mine' with a toothbrush and towel, and one labelled 'we can share' with a bucket and mug.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them into two groups.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the things. 2. Your child picks each one up and says what it is for.
flow.say: What is this for? And this? Which part of your body does each one keep clean?
flow.kid: Pick up each thing. What is it for? Which part of you does it clean?

ask.q: What is a nail cutter for?
good: So dirt can't hide under them.

flow.do: Your child sorts the things into 'only mine' and 'we can share'. Talk about each choice.
flow.say: Which of these should only you use? Which can the family share? Why?
flow.kid: Put each thing in a group: only mine, or we can share. Say why.

ask.q: Why should only you use your toothbrush?
good: The tiny beings from my mouth are on it.

flow.parent: A toothbrush should never be shared, because it carries the bacteria and any blood from one mouth to another. Towels are best kept one each. A bucket, mug and soap bar are usually shared, and are rinsed after use.

projects.title: My Clean Week chart
projects.context: In this project you colour a chart every day for a week. It shows when you brushed, bathed and washed your hands before meals.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a grid: 7 columns for the days, and 4 rows for morning brush, night brush, bath, and hands before meals
crayons

schedule.what: Draw the chart. Draw a picture at the start of each row. Colour today's boxes.
Colour today's boxes. Which row is hardest to remember?
Colour the last boxes. Count the coloured boxes in each row.

projects.record: The coloured chart, with one sentence said to a grown-up about the hardest row.

setup.art: A paper grid with seven columns and four rows, with a small drawing at the start of each row: a sun with a toothbrush, a moon with a toothbrush, a bucket, and a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the chart with four rows.

setup.art: A child colouring boxes on the chart at bedtime.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the boxes every evening for a week.

flow.do: 1. Draw the grid with your child. 2. They draw a small picture at the start of each row. 3. Colour today's boxes at bedtime.
flow.say: This chart shows a whole week of keeping clean. Each night we colour what you did today.
flow.kid: Draw a picture for each row. Tonight, colour what you did today.

flow.do: Each evening, from day 2 to day 6, your child colours the boxes for that day.
flow.say: What did you do today? Colour those boxes.
flow.kid: Colour today's boxes. Did you brush at night yet?
flow.wait: Colour a little every evening for six days.
flow.parent: Keep it light. An empty box is not a failure. It is a clue about what is easy to forget.

flow.do: On day 7, count the coloured boxes in each row together.
flow.say: Let's count each row. Which row has the most? Which has the fewest? Why do you think that one was harder?
flow.kid: Count each row. Which row has the most? Which is hardest to remember?

ask.q: Why was that row the hardest?

challenges.title: The Two-Minute Brush
challenges.context: Dentists say to brush for about two minutes. But two minutes is hard to feel. This challenge is to find a way to know when two minutes of brushing are up.
challenges.problem: Find a way to brush for about two minutes, and to give every part of your mouth a fair share of the time.
constraints: It must work at the sink, with wet hands.
It must use things from home.
Every part of the mouth must get a turn: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right.
materials: a clock or phone timer, to test your idea once
things from home, such as a small plastic bottle, a song or a set of beads
general: Use a phone timer or a clock.
Use a small sand timer, if you have one from a game.
Sing a song that lasts about two minutes.
creative: Count 30 slow brushes on each of the four parts of your mouth.
Make a song with four verses, one for each part of the mouth. Sing it in your head while you brush.
Ask a grown-up to make a tiny hole in the bottom of a small plastic bottle. Fill it with water. Find out how full it should be so that it takes two minutes to empty.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own two-minute brush plan. Test it once with a clock. Did it last two minutes? Was every part of your mouth brushed?

setup.art: A mouth drawn as a circle cut into four parts: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right, with a small toothbrush in each.
setup.caption: 1. Split your mouth into four parts.

setup.art: A child brushing at a sink while a grown-up holds a phone timer showing two minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Test your plan once with a clock.

flow.do: 1. Brush once without any timer. 2. A grown-up times it secretly.
flow.say: Brush your teeth the way you always do. I will time you, but I won't say how long.
flow.kid: Brush the way you always do. A grown-up times you secretly.
flow.parent: Most young children brush for well under a minute when nobody is timing.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child how long they brushed. 2. Talk about ideas for knowing when two minutes are up.
flow.say: You brushed for this long. Dentists say about two minutes. How could you know when two minutes are up, without looking at a clock?
flow.kid: How long did you brush? How could you know when two minutes are up?

good: Do each part of my mouth in turn.

flow.do: Try your child's idea once, and time it with a clock.
flow.say: Let's try your idea. I'll time it. Did it take about two minutes? Did every part get a turn?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Did it take two minutes? Did every part of your mouth get a turn?

challenges.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the bottle.

quiz.p: When should you wash your hands with soap?
opts: Before eating and after the toilet
quiz.why: Germs are too small to see, so hands can carry them even when they look clean. Before eating and after the toilet are the most important times.

quiz.p: How long should you rub soap on your hands?
opts: About 20 seconds, like singing Happy Birthday twice
quiz.why: About 20 seconds gives enough time to rub every part. One second misses most of the hand, and ten minutes is far more than needed.

quiz.p: In the biscuit test, where did the crumbs stay after the water rinse?
opts: In the grooves of the back teeth
quiz.why: Water runs over the top of the back teeth without reaching into the grooves. Only the bristles of a brush reach in.

quiz.p: Which of these should only you use?
quiz.why: A toothbrush goes in your mouth and carries the tiny beings from your mouth. So everyone has their own.

quiz.p: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
quiz.why: Plaque grows back all the time, so dentists say to brush twice a day, for about two minutes, morning and night.

quiz.p: What do the tiny living beings in your mouth eat?
quiz.why: They eat leftover food on your teeth. As they eat sugar, they make an acid, and the acid can wear a hole in a tooth over time. They do not eat the tooth itself.

quiz.p: Most of the tiny living beings on your skin and in your mouth are...
quiz.why: Only a few kinds make us ill. Most live with us quietly, and some help keep harmful ones away.

quiz.p: Why do we take a bath?
opts: To wash off sweat, dust and old skin
To make our skin grow longer

applications: Doctors and nurses wash their hands between every patient, so they do not carry germs from one person to the next.
Cooks in restaurants and in school kitchens wash their hands before touching food.

open_questions.q: How do the bacteria in plaque decide when to build their sticky layer?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria send each other chemical signals, and act together when there are many of them. Scientists are still working out how this works in a real mouth, with many kinds living together.

open_questions.q: Is a little contact with dirt and soil good for a child?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find that children who meet more of nature's microbes get some allergies less often. Scientists still argue about why, and which kinds of contact help.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be one of the tiny beings who live in a mouth?
open_questions.why_open: They sense food, acid and each other, and they act on what they sense. What that is like for them, nobody knows.

maths.problem: In the biscuit test, you looked at 4 back teeth. After a water rinse, 3 of them still had crumbs in the grooves. How many were clean?
maths.explain: Take the 3 teeth with crumbs away from the 4 teeth, and 1 is left. So most of the back teeth kept crumbs after the rinse.
maths.context: This is about the biscuit test, where you ate a biscuit and looked at your teeth after a water rinse.
maths.why_maths: Counting the teeth that kept crumbs shows how often water missed the grooves.

maths.problem: You brush your teeth 2 times every day. How many times do you brush in 3 days?
maths.explain: 2 and 2 and 2 make 6. Count in twos: 2, 4, 6.
maths.context: This is about the Clean Week chart, where you colour a box each time you brush.
maths.why_maths: Counting in twos shows how quickly brushing adds up when you do it morning and night.

maths.problem: On the Clean Week chart, the morning brush row has 7 coloured boxes, and the night brush row has 5. Which row is harder to remember? How do you know?
maths.answer: The night brush row. It has fewer coloured boxes: 5 is less than 7.
maths.explain: 7 is more than 5, so the morning brush was done more often. The row with fewer boxes is the one that was forgotten more.
maths.context: This is about the Clean Week chart.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two rows shows which habit needs help.

maths.problem: Your mouth has 4 parts: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right. You brush each part for 30 counts. In what order can you go round the mouth, so that no part is missed?
maths.answer: Any order that visits each of the 4 parts once, for example top left, top right, bottom right, bottom left.
maths.explain: There are many right answers. A good one goes round in a circle, so you always know which part comes next and none is missed.
maths.context: This is about the Two-Minute Brush challenge, where you split your mouth into four parts.
maths.why_maths: Using left, right, top and bottom helps you plan a path round the mouth that misses nothing.

Hygiene and 'old friends' hypotheses: D. Strachan, BMJ, 1989, and later work by G. Rook. Still debated.

roots.context: In the Biscuit Test, we looked into our own mouths and found where food stays after we eat. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves, and about the tiny living beings who share our bodies.

deep_truth.truth: In the biscuit test, crumbs stayed in the grooves of your back teeth after a rinse. Tiny living beings in your mouth eat those leftovers. So every time you eat, you feed them too. Brushing takes their leftovers away, so they make less of the acid that wears teeth.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a meal as ours alone, and of our mouth as only ours. But many kinds of living beings share every meal we eat, right there on our teeth.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Biscuit Test, crumbs stayed in the grooves of the back teeth after a water rinse, and only the brush took them out. In the Morning Tongue Test, the fuzzy plaque was back every morning, built overnight by the bacteria who live in the mouth.

three.who_am_i: You are a home. Many kinds of tiny living beings live in your mouth and on your skin.
three.what_is_life: Every living being eats and keeps their body in order: a bacterium, a cat licking her fur, and you with your toothbrush.
three.what_is_this_world: The water that washes you came from rain and rivers. It goes back to them, carrying what it washed off you.

roots.thread: One meal feeds many lives at once. The rice on your plate feeds you, and the crumbs left on your teeth feed the bacteria in your mouth. Your body is a home where many kinds of tiny living beings live. Keeping clean does not remove all of them. It keeps their numbers small, and keeps the harmful kinds out of your mouth.

teachings.teaching: Water makes the outside of the body clean. Truthfulness makes the inside clean.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar knew that water cleans the outside of the body. In the white cloth test, the bath water carried away dust we could not even see.

teachings.teaching: Water flows from high in the mountains, and runs deep in the Earth. It comes to us, and keeps all life going.
teachings.link: The water in your tap came a long way, from rain and rivers, before it washed your hands. Every time you wash your hands, you use that water.

science.text: Scientists have found more than 700 kinds of bacteria in human mouths. One person carries many dozens of kinds at a time.
Bacteria send each other chemical signals, and build a sticky layer like plaque when there are many of them. How they do this together in a real mouth is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Many microbiologists describe bacterial signals as chemistry that runs by itself, the way a match lights when it is struck. They say bacteria react to chemicals, but do not make choices.

how_we_found_out.context: What really makes holes in teeth? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people in many lands believed a toothache came from a tiny worm inside the tooth. An old clay tablet from Babylon tells of the tooth worm. In Europe, many people still believed it about 300 years ago. Then, in 1683, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek looked at the white paste from his own teeth. He was a cloth seller in the Netherlands who made his own tiny microscopes. He mixed the paste with clean water. He saw a great many tiny living beings, moving about. Nobody had ever seen them before. He found no tooth worm. About 200 years later, in 1890, a dentist called Willoughby Miller tested what these beings do. In his laboratory he gave them sugar and bread, and they made an acid. The acid softened pieces of tooth. So a hole in a tooth is not made by a worm. It is made by acid from the bacteria in plaque, who eat our leftover food.
how_we_found_out.who: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller who made his own microscopes, and later the dentist Willoughby Miller
how_we_found_out.when: Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria from his teeth in 1683. Miller showed that mouth bacteria make acid from sugar in 1890.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That holes in teeth are made by a tooth worm. No one ever found a tooth worm. Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living beings in plaque instead, and Miller showed that their acid softens teeth.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in a long old-fashioned coat holding a tiny hand-held microscope up to his eye by a window, with a small dish of water on the table.
